name: Spanish Florida
info: Spain's province of La Florida in south-eastern North America, centred on St. Augustine, a strategic buffer of forts and Franciscan missions that passed to Britain in 1763 and to the United States in 1821.

facts.capital: St. Augustine (San Agustín); in the second Spanish period East Florida from St. Augustine and West Florida from Pensacola
facts.founder: Pedro Menéndez de Avilés, Adelantado of Florida, who founded St. Augustine in 1565; Juan Ponce de León had claimed the land for Spain in 1513
facts.predecessor: The Timucua, Calusa, Tequesta, Apalachee, Tocobaga, Ais and other native peoples; French Florida (Fort Caroline); British East and West Florida (1763–1783) before the second Spanish period
facts.successor: Great Britain's East and West Florida (1763); the United States (the Mobile District by 1812, the rest of Florida in 1821)

t: Spain held Florida less for its wealth, since it found no gold or silver there, than as a fortified buffer between New Spain and the English colonies to the north.

Disease, war and the raids of Carolina colonists and their native allies destroyed the native peoples and the Franciscan missions, and Creek refugees and people fleeing slavery later formed the Seminole culture in the emptied land.
From 1693 the Spanish Crown freed enslaved people who fled to Florida and accepted baptism, and a free black militia garrisoned Fort Mose near St. Augustine.
dyk: The marriage of Luisa de Abrego, a free black domestic servant from Seville, and Miguel Rodríguez, a Segovian conquistador, in St. Augustine in 1565 is the first known and recorded Christian marriage in what is now the continental United States.
ev: Juan Ponce de León claims the land for Spain and names it La Florida, for the Easter season of Pascua Florida
Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founds St. Augustine, overwhelms the French Fort Caroline and has the shipwrecked Huguenots executed at Matanzas
The English privateer Francis Drake plunders and burns St. Augustine
The Castillo de San Marcos is built at St. Augustine, with forced labour from the Timucuan, Guale and Apalache peoples
James Moore's Carolina army razes the town of St. Augustine and then destroys most of the Apalachee missions
Spain trades Florida to Great Britain for Havana and Manila, and the Spanish population of St. Augustine emigrates to Cuba
The Peace of Paris returns East and West Florida to Spain, without specifying their boundaries
The Adams–Onís Treaty cedes Florida to the United States; it takes effect on 17 July 1821

sections.foundation:
Juan Ponce de León, governor of Puerto Rico, sighted the east coast of the peninsula in April 1513, claimed it for Spain and named it La Florida, for the season of Pascua Florida. The legend that he sought a Fountain of Youth arose long after his death; like other conquistadors he was most likely looking for gold, land to rule and Indians to convert or enslave. Spanish raiders had probably already enslaved people on the coast. The expeditions of Pánfilo de Narváez, who landed near Tampa Bay in 1528, and Hernando de Soto, who marched from Tampa Bay in 1539 as far as the Mississippi, found no riches, and attempts to settle, at San Miguel de Gualdape in 1526 and at Ochuse and Santa Elena under Tristán de Luna y Arellano in 1559, ended in failure.

Permanent settlement answered French Florida. After René Goulaine de Laudonnière founded Fort Caroline for Huguenot colonists in 1564, King Philip II appointed Pedro Menéndez de Avilés Adelantado of Florida, with a commission to drive out non-Spanish adventurers. On 8 September 1565 Menéndez landed with settlers to found St. Augustine and the Mission Nombre de Dios. He overwhelmed Fort Caroline, sparing only the women and children, and ordered the shipwrecked Huguenots of Jean Ribault's fleet executed at the place called Matanzas.
sections.socioeconomy:
With no gold or silver, and a native population too reduced by disease and slave raids for an encomienda system of forced farm labour, Spanish Florida had no large plantations. Free-range cattle ranches in north-central Florida were its most successful enterprise, supplying local and Cuban markets; Francisco Menéndez Márquez founded the largest. From the 1630s a chain of missions from St. Augustine to the panhandle sent maize and other food to the town, and Apalachee men from the missions had to work there every year. The ports of St. Augustine and Pensacola served Spanish ships in need of water and supplies.

Spanish men married or had unions with Pensacola, Creek and African women, slave and free, and their children formed a mestizo and mulatto population. Spain encouraged people enslaved in the southern colonies to come to Florida as a refuge: St. Augustine had an all-black militia by 1683, and in 1693 King Charles II proclaimed free all who fled to Florida and accepted conversion and baptism. A free black population grew in St. Augustine, and Fort Mose was settled by free black militiamen and their families. Spain ended the policy in 1790, but people fleeing slavery kept crossing the border to settle near Seminole villages.
sections.military:
The colony's defence rested on a few fortified towns. In 1586 Francis Drake plundered and burned St. Augustine on his way back from raiding Santo Domingo and Cartagena, exposing Spain's inability to defend its settlements. From 1672 the Castillo de San Marcos was built there with the forced labour of Timucuan, Guale and Apalache people, its first stage completed in 1695, with Fort Matanzas to the south to watch the sea. In 1702 James Moore's army of Carolina colonists and Yamasee, Tallapoosa, Alabama and other Creek warriors razed the town but could not take the fort; in 1704 his raids into Apalachee Province destroyed most of the remaining missions and killed or enslaved most of their people.

On the Gulf coast Spain tried to block French expansion from Louisiana. It founded the Presidio Santa Maria de Galve on Pensacola Bay in 1696 and a presidio on St. Joseph Bay in 1701; the French took both in 1718 and 1719, and Spain regained Pensacola Bay in 1722. In the War of Jenkins' Ear (1739–1748) a British attack on St. Augustine and a Spanish invasion of Georgia were both repulsed. By the early 19th century there were only about 500 Spanish troops in West Florida, and in 1814 the Spanish governor at Pensacola let British forces land to arm the Creeks against the United States.
sections.governance:
La Florida formed part of the Captaincy General of Cuba in the Viceroyalty of New Spain. Its governor sat at St. Augustine, but the Gulf presidios founded from 1696 were placed directly under the Viceroy of New Spain, while the Presidio San Marcos de Apalachee, founded in 1718, answered to the governor. Several governors and officials were born in the province, among them Nicolás Ponce de León II, acting governor in the 1660s and 1670s, and Pedro Benedit Horruytiner, governor from 1651 to 1654.

Spanish control rested on alliances with native caciques, who allied with the Spanish to strengthen their power, gain protection against rivals and acquire goods; these alliances were unstable. Governor Pedro de Ibarra sought peace with the peoples south of St. Augustine and in 1605 sent the cartographer Álvaro Mexía to the Ais. The missions were the other instrument of rule: the Jesuits began them in 1567 and withdrew in 1572, and from 1573 the Franciscans ran dozens among the Guale, Timucua and Apalachee. The Guale rebelled in 1597, the Apalachee in February 1647, after which their men were forced to work on public projects and Spanish ranches, and the Timucua in 1656. In the second Spanish period Spain kept the British division into East and West Florida, and in 1785 moved their border east to the Suwannee River.
sections.impact:
La Florida was the first major European land claim and attempted settlement in northern America. Spain's claim, resting on the 16th-century expeditions, once reached over much of the present south-eastern United States, and Juan Pardo's expeditions from Santa Elena in 1566–1568 went as far as eastern Tennessee. St. Augustine is the oldest continuously inhabited European-established settlement in the continental United States, and Mission Nombre de Dios was perhaps the first mission there.

For the native peoples Spanish rule meant war, forced labour and, above all, epidemic disease. The Timucua, Calusa, Tequesta, Apalachee, Tocobaga and Ais, most of whom had resisted the Spanish, declined drastically, and by the early 1700s large parts of the peninsula were nearly empty. Creek and other refugees driven from their lands by the Carolina settlements moved south into this land in the 18th century, joined by African Americans fleeing slavery; with perhaps a few descendants of the older peoples they formed a new Seminole culture. Under pressure from settlers and the Seminole Wars the Seminole later moved into central and southern Florida. The colony's role as a refuge from slavery made it a source of conflict with the southern colonies and then with the United States.
sections.decline:
Spanish Florida shrank from the 1600s as native depopulation emptied the missions. From 1680 Carolina colonists and their allies attacked mission villages, and after Moore's raids of 1702–1704 the missionaries abandoned their outposts in 1706. The Province of Carolina, French New Orleans from 1718 and Georgia from 1732 hemmed in its borders. In 1763 Spain traded Florida to Great Britain for Havana and Manila, and the entire Spanish population of St. Augustine left for Cuba. Spain recaptured most of West Florida in the American Revolutionary War, and the Peace of Paris of 1783 returned both Floridas to it.

The ill-defined borders brought a dispute with the United States, settled at the 31st parallel by Pinckney's Treaty of 1795. The United States intervened in a West Florida uprising in 1810, absorbed the Mobile District by 1812, and quietly supported the Patriot War of East Florida of 1810–1812. American slave-hunters raided Black Seminole villages; the 'Negro Fort' at Prospect Bluff was destroyed by an American attack in 1816, and Andrew Jackson's campaign of 1817–1818, the First Seminole War, occupied Pensacola. Unable to defend the territory, Spain negotiated: the Adams–Onís Treaty of 22 February 1819 took effect on 17 July 1821, and hundreds of Black Seminoles sailed from Cape Florida to the Bahamas to avoid being returned to bondage.

summary: Spanish Florida was founded at St. Augustine in 1565 to keep the French and English from the routes of New Spain. Without gold or a large labour force it remained a buffer of forts, missions and cattle ranches; its native peoples were destroyed by disease and slave raids, and after a British interlude it passed to the United States in 1821.
references: Jerald T. Milanich, Florida Indians and the Invasion from Europe (University Press of Florida, 1995)
Amy Turner Bushnell, The King's Coffer: Proprietors of the Spanish Florida Treasury 1565–1702 (University of Florida Press, 1981)
Jane G. Landers, Atlantic Creoles in the Age of Revolutions (Harvard University Press, 2010)
Nathaniel Millett, The Maroons of Prospect Bluff and Their Quest for Freedom in the Atlantic World (University Press of Florida, 2013)
Rembert W. Patrick, Florida Fiasco: Rampant Rebels on the Georgia-Florida Border, 1810–1815 (University of Georgia Press, 1954)
Charlton Tebeau, A History of Florida (University of Miami Press, 1980)

pointDescs.1565: Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founds St. Augustine and Mission Nombre de Dios, takes Fort Caroline and executes the Huguenots at Matanzas.
pointDescs.1566: The colony of Santa Elena is founded on Parris Island, and Juan Pardo's expeditions of 1566–1568 reach eastern Tennessee.
pointDescs.1572: The Jesuits withdraw from their Florida missions after hostile encounters; the Franciscans take over in 1573.
pointDescs.1586: Francis Drake plunders and burns St. Augustine; Santa Elena is abandoned the next year.
pointDescs.1605: Governor Pedro de Ibarra pursues peace with the peoples south of St. Augustine and sends Álvaro Mexía to the Ais.
pointDescs.1647: The Franciscan missions, spreading since the 1630s, feed St. Augustine; after the Apalachee revolt of February their men are forced to work in the town and on ranches.
pointDescs.1672: Construction of the Castillo de San Marcos begins with native forced labour; the mission chain and the cattle ranches are at their height before the Carolina raids of 1680.
pointDescs.1693: King Charles II frees all enslaved people who flee to Florida and accept baptism; the first stage of the Castillo is completed in 1695.
pointDescs.1698: Pensacola is founded on the western panhandle, strengthening the Spanish claim against the French.
pointDescs.1702: James Moore's army razes the town of St. Augustine but cannot take the Castillo.
pointDescs.1704: Moore's raids destroy most of the Apalachee missions and kill or enslave most of their people; by 1706 the missionaries have withdrawn.
pointDescs.1719: The French take Santa Maria de Galve on Pensacola Bay, a year after Bahía San José de Valladares.
pointDescs.1722: Spain regains the Pensacola Bay area from the French.
pointDescs.1739: The War of Jenkins' Ear begins; a British attack on St. Augustine is repulsed, and the war ends with the northern border near Florida's present one.
pointDescs.1763: Spain trades Florida to Great Britain for Havana and Manila, and the Spanish population leaves for Cuba.
pointDescs.1783: The Peace of Paris returns East and West Florida to Spain, which governs them as separate provinces.
pointDescs.1795: Pinckney's Treaty sets the border with the United States at the 31st parallel and opens the Mississippi to American navigation.
pointDescs.1812: After intervening in a West Florida uprising in 1810, the United States absorbs the Mobile District; the Patriot War unsettles East Florida.
pointDescs.1818: Andrew Jackson's campaign in the First Seminole War occupies Pensacola; by 1819 the United States effectively controls much of the panhandle.
pointDescs.1821: The Adams–Onís Treaty takes effect on 17 July and Spanish Florida ceases to exist.

notes: The register's span 1565–1821 includes the British period of 1763–1783; the curve marks it with the 1763 and 1783 points only. The article dates the claim to 1513 (Ponce de León), given as an event before the register's start.
The article dates the Province of Carolina once to 1663 (charter) and once to 1639 'by the English'; the 1639 date is not used and Carolina is left undated in the decline section.
The article gives Pensacola's founding as 1698 in one place and the Presidio Santa Maria de Galve on Pensacola Bay as 1696 in another; both are kept where the article puts them.
The peak of the curve (1672) is a judgement: the mission chain from the 1630s and the Castillo's start, before the Carolina raids from 1680; the article gives no single peak.
Martín de Argüelles, the de Soto/Narváez details and the War of 1812 episodes (Woodbine, Nicolls, Fort Bowyer) are mostly left out for length.
